description: building an interactive web platform for the Lunar Landing Site Navigator challenge.
summary:
Lunar Landing Site Navigator is an interactive decision-support prototype designed to help users explore and compare candidate landing locations near the Moon's south pole. The region presents challenging illumination and communication conditions, making it important to understand how local terrain affects the visibility of the Sun and Earth over time.

Our application combines NASA's Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter (LOLA) elevation data with SPICE-based celestial geometry to calculate terrain horizons and estimate the apparent-disc visibility of the Sun and Earth at selected locations. Users can compare three candidate sites, explore time-dependent visibility, examine potential visibility windows, and adjust mission priorities through a configurable scoring system.

By bringing terrain analysis, celestial geometry and mission-oriented comparisons into one accessible interface, Lunar Landing Site Navigator makes lunar south-pole environmental constraints easier to explore and understand. It is an exploratory planning tool, not a landing-safety certification or operational power and communications simulator.
details:
Lunar Landing Site Navigator

The Challenge

The lunar south pole is an important region for future lunar exploration, but evaluating candidate landing locations is challenging. Local terrain can obstruct sunlight and the line of sight to Earth. These conditions change with time and can influence solar-energy opportunities and potential communication windows.

Our project addresses this challenge by bringing terrain-aware celestial visibility analysis and candidate-site comparison into one interactive application.

Our Solution

Lunar Landing Site Navigator is an interactive decision-support prototype for exploring candidate landing locations near the lunar south pole. It currently evaluates three illustrative candidate locations and allows users to compare their terrain and visibility characteristics.

The application combines NASA's Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter (LOLA) elevation data with NASA/JPL SPICE geometry to estimate the directions of the Sun and Earth relative to each lunar surface location.

How It Works

1. Lunar terrain analysis

The application uses an 80 m/pixel LOLA south-polar digital elevation model. It samples the surrounding terrain along multiple azimuth directions to construct a local horizon profile. This profile represents the elevation angle of terrain that may obstruct a target.

2. Sun and Earth geometry

SPICE kernels provide the planetary and lunar geometry used to calculate the apparent directions of the Sun and Earth. These directions are transformed into a local east-north-up coordinate frame, allowing azimuth and elevation to be evaluated from each candidate site.

3. Terrain-aware apparent-disc visibility

Instead of treating the Sun and Earth as dimensionless points, the application samples points across their apparent discs. Each sampled direction is compared with the local terrain horizon. The resulting visible fraction indicates how much of the sampled apparent disc is unobstructed.

4. Time-dependent analysis

Precomputed observations cover approximately 30 days, from November 15 to December 15, 2026, at a nominal two-hour cadence. Users can examine visibility patterns and sampled visibility windows for each candidate location.

5. Configurable mission comparison

The Mission Planner combines seven metrics: six temporal visibility fractions and one spatial terrain-openness measure. Users can adjust metric weights and configure minimum thresholds to explore different mission priorities. The resulting scores are comparative decision-support indicators, not official landing-site suitability ratings.

What Makes It Useful and Creative

The project integrates terrain elevation, celestial geometry, apparent-disc visibility, time-series analysis and configurable mission priorities in a single accessible interface. It helps users explore trade-offs between candidate locations instead of relying on a single illumination or visibility measurement.

The application is designed to make complex lunar environmental analysis easier to explore for students, educators and people interested in lunar mission planning.

Technology Stack

  • Programming: Python
  • Scientific computing: NumPy, SciPy and Pandas
  • Geospatial processing: GDAL and Rasterio
  • Celestial geometry: SpiceyPy and NASA/JPL SPICE kernels
  • Backend: FastAPI
  • Frontend: React, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Framer Motion and Lucide React
  • Testing: pytest

Limitations and Future Development

The current prototype uses an 80 m/pixel terrain model, finite apparent-disc sampling and a nominal two-hour observation cadence. Short visibility intervals may therefore be missed, and small-scale terrain features may not be resolved.

Sun visibility is not a complete electrical-power model, Earth visibility does not guarantee a viable radio link, and terrain openness does not establish landing safety. The candidate-site scores depend on user-defined weights and thresholds and should not be interpreted as official NASA criteria.

Future development could incorporate higher-resolution local terrain, solar-power and thermal models, communication link budgets, landing-hazard assessment and additional candidate locations.

Intended Impact

Lunar Landing Site Navigator demonstrates how open NASA data and scientific computing can be combined into an understandable exploratory tool. It aims to help users visualize lunar south-pole environmental constraints, compare candidate locations and better understand the trade-offs involved in early mission-planning studies.
